summary:
Bengkulu is a province of Indonesia, and trans visitors here stand under Indonesia's national legal and policy framework. No Bengkulu-specific statute, enforcement action, protection measure, service or documented incident directed at trans people appears in the sources; the province is therefore assessed on national conditions.

Consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults is not itself criminalised in private in Indonesia outside the provinces with their own provisions. There are, however, no anti-discrimination protections for lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender people anywhere in the country.

The amended national penal code, signed in December 2022, took effect on 2 January 2026. Its provision on consensual sex outside marriage is the principal route by which same-sex activity becomes prosecutable, because Indonesia does not permit same-sex marriage and so no same-sex relationship can be registered as marital. Reporting on the provision describes the penalty as up to two years' imprisonment, while the national rights overview in the sources gives up to one year and records that the offence is actionable on the complaint of an immediate family member. The sources do not reconcile the two figures. Prosecutions reported to date are selective rather than systematic, and police and prosecutors have discretion over whether a complaint proceeds.

Legal gender recognition remains the hardest documentary requirement facing a trans visitor. Changing one's gender marker on Indonesian identity documents requires sex-reassignment surgery plus the approval of a judge. A trans person whose documents do not match their presentation carries a documentary exposure at checkpoints, immigration counters and hotels that has no non-surgical alternative route.

Two provinces maintain their own criminal provisions against same-sex sexual activity between men and between women: Aceh, where Sharia law applies and punishments are imposed under provincial religious law, and South Sumatra. Aceh's sanctions reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. In Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025.

Police raids on LGBTQ+ venues and gatherings are a live enforcement mechanism. On 22 June 2025 Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering had violated no law. On 11 August 2025 three men were arrested over a Facebook community page.

Vigilante violence against trans people has intensified alongside official framing. A wave of mob attacks on transgender women swept Indonesia between 14 and 16 July 2026; in Bogor more than fifteen trans women were doused, stripped and beaten, and footage of the assaults was circulated online. Reporting from August 2026 ties that wave to a presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025, which lists 'the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture' among nonmilitary threats to be monitored and controlled alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy. Researchers cited in the same reporting document markedly hardened anti-queer public attitudes since 2016.

Hostility in this environment has produced fatal outcomes for foreign trans people. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. Authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release, according to a call made to his mother in Lima. He died in custody. His mother alleges that police beat him; Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Public opinion is strongly aligned with the official position. A 2025 Pew survey found that 93% of Indonesians rated homosexuality morally unacceptable. Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025.
tangentialFactors:
The regional pattern cuts both ways and a visitor should not assume the national picture applies uniformly. Aceh's caning of two men in February 2025 and South Sumatra's own criminal provisions show that provincial religious and moral law can be materially harsher than the national code, and that enforcement reaches visitors physically present in the province. Bengkulu carries no equivalent documented provision, but the sources do not positively establish that none exists.

State violence against foreign trans people is not confined to fines or detention conditions. The 2022 custody death of Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla involved an alleged demand of up to US$100,000 for release, an amount that bears on how a trans traveller should expect arrest to be handled if it occurs.

The October 2025 presidential decree changed the status of LGBTQ+ people from a moral question to a national defence question. That reframing is what reporting links to the July 2026 vigilante wave, and it means hostility may originate from civilian mobs as well as from police and prosecutors.
localsOnly:
Indonesian citizens cannot change their gender marker on identity documents without undergoing sex-reassignment surgery and obtaining a judge's approval. There is no administrative or self-declaration route, and the requirement places surgical and financial barriers on residents as well as on visitors.

Indonesians live under a penal code provision criminalising consensual sex outside marriage, actionable on the complaint of an immediate family member. Because same-sex marriage is not available, the provision applies to same-sex relationships regardless of whether both parties consent, and it can be triggered by family members rather than by police initiative.

There are no national anti-discrimination protections covering sexual orientation or gender identity for residents, workers, patients or students. Public opinion data from 2025 shows 93% of the population regarding homosexuality as morally unacceptable, which shapes what a trans Indonesian can expect in housing, employment and healthcare access even where no law restricts them.

Residents in Aceh and South Sumatra face provincial criminal provisions on same-sex sexual activity in addition to national law. In Aceh, which applies Sharia law, punishments are imposed under provincial religious authority and were applied publicly in February 2025. Attacks on trans women in July 2026 were filmed and circulated online by members of the public.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not agree on the penalty attached to the 2022 penal-code provision on consensual sex outside marriage: one source gives up to two years' imprisonment, the national rights overview in the sources gives up to one year. The figure should be verified against the statute text before it is cited as settled.

Whether Bengkulu province has enacted its own moral or criminal provisions equivalent to those of Aceh and South Sumatra is unresolved. No source in the inventory addresses provincial legislation for Bengkulu, and the absence of a documented provision is not evidence that none exists.

No Bengkulu-specific data exists on enforcement of the 2026 penal-code provision, on police treatment of trans people in the province, on access to gender-affirming healthcare or on hate-crime reporting. None of these were sourced for this jurisdiction.

The status of the 2025 arrests over a Facebook community page, including charges and outcomes, is not documented in the sources. The same is true of any prosecution brought under the new penal code since 2 January 2026.
